_comment: The SCA dependency audit, driven by the faked network below. tiny-obscure-helper is pinned and resolvable but nobody uses it (12 downloads a month), so unpopular-source-dependency rejects: a dependency the reviewer cannot lean on the community for must be shipped readable instead. vitest is a devDependency, never shipped - but the reviewer BUILDS from this source, so a vulnerable build tool runs on their machine and vendor-vulnerable-dev reports it. It is popularity-gated for the same reason, though this fixture does not exercise that: the network map answers a downloads lookup for tiny-obscure-helper only, so vitest's 404s and records nothing. The dev-dependency popularity gate is unit-covered instead (tests/unit/vendor-verify.test.js). The OSV stub answers ONE body for the endpoint, so both queries see the same advisory and the shipped dependency is reported by vendor-vulnerable as well - which is why the advisory here names no affected package: a fixture cannot claim an advisory belongs to a specific one while answering every query with it. The XPI-side twin (vendor-vulnerable) pins the affected/fixed-version mapping instead. platform-binary is an optionalDependency, and is audited exactly as the devDependency is: npm installs one where the platform allows, so it too runs on the reviewer's machine during the build. It is the entry that would fall between two stools if this map were left unclassified - the lock's own direct-dependency set spans every declaration map, so the whole-tree audit skips it as DECLARED, and nothing else would receive it. The committed package-lock.json is not what this fixture is about: a source archive declaring dependencies owes one (sca-lock-file-missing), and it restates both declarations faithfully so sca-lock-file-invalid stays silent too.
